source.title: Open problems in graph theory. II: On the achromatic number of a graph

accepted.question_text: Given a finite tree T = (V,E) and a positive integer K, does T admit a complete K-coloring, meaning a coloring of the vertices of T with colors {1,2,...,K} such that adjacent vertices receive different colors and, for every pair i,j of distinct colors, some edge of T has one endpoint colored i and the other endpoint colored j?
accepted.context_brief: Achromatic number decision problem for trees

evidence.quote: INSTANCE: A tree T = (V,E), a positive integer K. QUESTION: Does T have a complete K-coloring? A coloring of the vertices of a tree T with K colors {1,2,...,K} is called complete if (i) adjacent vertices are assigned different colors, and (ii) for every pair i,j of distinct colors there exists a pair of adjacent vertices colored i and j.

UPDATE: this problem has been shown to be NP-complete for trees; I will provide the reference shortly. It now remains to determine for what classes of trees can the achromatic number be determined in polynomial time.

accepted.question_text: For which classes of finite trees can the achromatic number be determined in polynomial time, where the achromatic number of a graph G is the maximum integer K for which G has a complete K-coloring, and a complete K-coloring is a vertex coloring with colors {1,2,...,K} in which adjacent vertices receive different colors and every pair of distinct colors appears on the endpoints of at least one edge?
accepted.context_brief: Polynomial-time classes for tree achromatic number

evidence.quote: The maximum integer K for which a graph G has a complete K-coloring is called the achromatic number of G. For many years it was not known whether the achromatic number of a tree can be found in polynomial time. It now remains to determine for what classes of trees can the achromatic number be determined in polynomial time.
